title: Need more magic
body:
Here’s the thing about habit-tracking apps: they all promise to fix your life. Track this, check that, and suddenly—poof—you’re a productivity ninja. 

Habits isn’t just any app, though. It’s clean, user-friendly, and genuinely helpful. But does it have that secret sauce that keeps you coming back, day after day? Well, not quite.

Let me break it down for you.

What Works:

	1.	Simplicity That Doesn’t Insult You
The interface is so intuitive, even your grandmother could use it to crush her knitting goals. No fluff, no fuss. Just pure, clean & fun design that gets out of your way.

	2.	Customizable Goals Without Overthinking
Want to drink more water? Meditate? Remember to floss? This app lets you set your own priorities instead of forcing you into a cookie-cutter system.

	3.	Feedback You Can Actually Use

There’s a small dopamine hit every time you check something off, and honestly, that’s what we’re all chasing, right?

Where It Falls Short

Here’s the kicker: Habits has everything you need—except the thing you actually need. It’s all surface-level. The app doesn’t go deep, and that’s a problem because building habits isn’t just about ticking boxes. It’s about systems.

What Could Be Better: 

	1.	Automate the “Why”
Right now, the app makes you think too hard about why you’re doing what you’re doing. A James Clear-inspired feature could help link new habits to existing ones. Call it a “habit stacker” or something.

	2.	The magic of reps

Habits misses the magic of streaks and reps—the lifeblood of habit-building. A simple feature to track and celebrate consecutive wins would make the app far more addictive. Think glowing chains or a progress bar that resets if you skip a day. 
Momentum matters, and without it, the app feels static, not dynamic.

	3.	Kill the Perfectionism 
Trap Miss a day? The app subtly guilt-trips you. Missing once is fine, twice not so much. The app needs to reinforce resilience, not rigid perfectionism.

Final Verdict

Habits is like the kid in class who always does their homework but never raises their hand. It’s solid, dependable, and you’d probably lend it your notes. But if it really wants to stand out, it needs to embrace the deeper psychology of habit formation.

Until then, it’s a good tool—but not a great one. Use it, enjoy it, but don’t be afraid to break out of it

Rating: 3.9
Clean, useful, but missing the heart of the matter.

body:

However, I have downloaded on iPhone and iPad and they dont link. So all of habits I spent time setting up on my phone version aren’t on the iPad version and there is nowhere to click to merge. 

This is very poor and pretty unique. Pretty much every app you download across macOS will automatically understand that you are the same user for example MyFitnessPal, Instagram and Microsoft apps.

Makes it unusable for me which is sad.

author: Giles H.

title: Works well to form habits, but why subscription based?
body:
This is one of the best habit tracking apps I've used. Cool interface, making you feel like you're on a journey to building a habit. It has made me stick to routines (working out, going for a walk, reading) that I wasn't able to do with willpower alone. I'd be happy to pay for it on that basis. 

What I don't understand is why this is subscription based. It doesn't seem like any new features get added over time. The data is (I assume) stored locally so there's no server costs. The subscription only gets you cosmetic items. Yet I'm shown ads asking me to subscribe every day I open the app. Unfortunately it's joined the current trend where every app needs to have a subscription, so I've docked it a star for that. If it wasn't for this, it'd be perfect.
